units.title: Partial failure, clocks and event ordering
outcomes: Explain why a timeout cannot distinguish a lost request, a paused node and a lost reply.
Assign physical and logical timestamps to a message history and identify causal and concurrent events.
Choose a local clock for elapsed time without treating it as a cross-machine ordering oracle.
units.why: Assume Programming's cancellation-timeouts-retries unit. Here the question is what the caller can know after a timeout, and which event orders remain defensible when clocks disagree.

next.note: Apply uncertain failure detection to replication and failover.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: uncertain outcomes and physical clocks
study.locator: Chapter 9, Faults and Partial Failures and Unreliable Networks, pp. 346 to 353; Unreliable Clocks through Timestamps for ordering events, pp. 358 to 364

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: causal order and logical clocks
study.locator: Chapter 6, The happens-before relation and concurrency, pp. 238 to 239, and Version vectors, p. 242; Chapter 10, Logical Clocks, pp. 420 to 422

focus: A timeout is an observation of silence, not proof of non-execution. Preserve an unknown outcome in the history.
Use monotonic time for local durations. Wall-clock readings can disagree across nodes; local monotonic readings have no shared epoch.
Happens-before follows process order, send-to-receive edges and transitivity. A smaller Lamport timestamp does not prove a causal dependency.
Distinguish scalar clocks that order events from vectors that can expose concurrency. Neither provides consensus or elapsed seconds.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, trace five events in this order: A sends m to B; C performs an unrelated local event; B receives m; B sends a reply to A; A receives it. Start all counters at zero, increment on each local/send event, and set a receive counter to max(local, received)+1. Get counters 1, 1, 2, 3, 4. Label the A-to-B-to-A chain and C's concurrent event. Use (counter, node ID) to break ties, but do not infer causality from that tie-break. Then draw two executions with the same caller history: P invokes write(x,1) and times out; in one the request is dropped, in the other S applies it and the reply is dropped. Check the clocks and indistinguishability by hand; the numbers are logical counters, not measured time.
traps: Comparing monotonic clock values from two hosts as if they were UTC timestamps.
Treating timestamp order as a proof of causality or as evidence that an acknowledged write is durable.
Interpreting a timeout as permission to repeat an externally visible effect without checking its identity.

selfTest.q: Can the caller tell a dropped request from a dropped reply after a timeout?
selfTest.a: Not from silence alone. The operation may have executed, so its outcome is unknown.

selfTest.q: If L(a) < L(b), must a happen before b?
selfTest.a: No. Causal order implies increasing Lamport counters, but unrelated events can also have different counters.

selfTest.q: What do vectors (2,1) and (1,2) tell you?
selfTest.a: Neither dominates the other componentwise. Under the vector algorithm's causal tracking assumptions, the represented events are concurrent.

selfTest.q: Does a monotonic clock make an expired lease safe?
selfTest.a: No. A process can pause or a request can be delayed after a lease check. The receiving resource must enforce ownership.

practice.name: Gossip Glomers Challenge 2: Unique ID Generation
practice.locator: Specification, RPC generate, and Evaluation with the unique-ids workload
practice.note: After Challenge 1 Echo in the simulation unit, implement IDs without assuming synchronized clocks. This is a learner-run challenge, not a run reported here. Java and Go are absent locally: use a JDK container such as eclipse-temurin:21 for Maelstrom and Python protocol nodes, or a separate Go build container for the tutorial. Follow the challenge's installation prerequisites. Explain why (node ID, counter) needs persistent counters or fresh incarnation IDs if restarts are added; the challenge does not crash nodes.

units.stopWhen: You recover the five counters without the source, distinguish the two timeout executions, and defend your ID scheme's uniqueness and restart assumptions.

fit.note: DDIA supplies uncertainty and clock mechanisms at derive depth; Unique ID Generation tests the distinction between uniqueness and time order.

units.title: Replication, quorums and consensus vocabulary
outcomes: Trace replication lag and acknowledged-write loss during asynchronous failover.
Derive quorum intersection and construct a stale-membership counterexample.
Separate consensus safety properties from termination assumptions and failure-detector suspicions.
units.why: Copies alone do not define which writes survive or which reads are fresh. Quorum arithmetic becomes useful only when membership, persisted acknowledgements and version comparison are explicit.

next.note: Name the histories that an intersecting replica set still does not rule out.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: leaders, lag and quorum limits
study.locator: Chapter 6, Single-Leader Replication and Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Replication, pp. 198 to 201; Handling Node Outages, pp. 204 to 206; Problems with Replication Lag, p. 209; Leaderless Replication through Understanding the limitations of quorum consistency, pp. 229 to 234

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: failure detection and consensus contract
study.locator: Chapter 9, Fault Detection and Timeouts and Unbounded Delays, pp. 351 to 353; Chapter 10, Consensus, pp. 425 to 429, through the single-value consensus properties
study.depth: Stop before Compare-and-set as consensus. Learn agreement, integrity, validity and conditional termination, not a Raft implementation. Timeouts alone do not guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous execution; practical progress needs additional assumptions such as eventual synchrony.

focus: State whether an acknowledgement means receipt, persistence or application at each replica. Asynchronous failover can discard acknowledged writes that never reached the promoted follower.
For a fixed replica universe of size n, |W intersect R| is at least w+r-n. This proves overlap, not a complete linearizability protocol.
Membership changes, forgotten acknowledged data, concurrent writes and faulty timestamp resolution can break the freshness argument.
Consensus agreement, integrity and validity are safety properties. Progress requires the protocol's fault and timing assumptions; a timeout supplies suspicion, not knowledge.
units.reproduce: By hand derive |W intersect R| >= w+r-n from |W union R| <= n. In Python 3.14, enumerate all size-three subsets of ABCDE and all 100 write/read pairs; the minimum intersection is one. Now construct this explicit history with initial x=0 everywhere: event 1, P invokes write(x,1) using old membership ABC; event 2, A and B persist 1 and P receives OK; event 3, Q invokes read(x) using new membership CDE, before state transfer; event 4, D and E reply 0 and Q returns 0. Both configurations have n=3,w=2,r=2, but W={A,B} and R={D,E} do not intersect. Check by hand that this violates linearizability: the completed write precedes the stale read. State why a coordinated membership transition is missing.
traps: Adding quorum sizes across different membership views as though they were subsets of one universe.
Calling a majority vote consensus without a protocol that preserves earlier decisions across leaders and restarts.
Calling leader receipt durable on a follower, or assuming replication replaces a backup.

selfTest.q: For n=5,w=3,r=3, what overlap is guaranteed?
selfTest.a: At least one replica, provided both sets belong to the same five-member configuration.
No. It proves set intersection. Version ordering, concurrent operations, read behavior, persistence and membership transitions still need a correct protocol.

selfTest.q: What happens if an asynchronous leader acknowledges a write, dies, and a follower without it is promoted?
selfTest.a: The acknowledged write can be lost from the surviving history. Local persistence on the old leader does not guarantee survival of that failover.

selfTest.q: Must a consensus group keep deciding during a permanent partition?
selfTest.a: Not unconditionally. Safety must be preserved, while termination depends on reachable participants and the protocol's timing assumptions.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: replica lag, persisted acknowledgements, node loss and a stale-membership history, with configuration IDs recorded in every operation.
units.stopWhen: You derive the intersection bound and explain exactly why the two-majority history violates linearizability without contradicting the bound.

fit.note: The selected DDIA sections cover leader failure, quorum derivation and consensus vocabulary; the mini-project supplies failure practice without implementing consensus.

units.title: Consistency models and conflict resolution
outcomes: Classify explicit histories under linearizable, causal, eventual and session contracts.
Distinguish serializable transactions from real-time ordered single-object operations.
Explain what last-write-wins discards and choose an application merge that preserves the required intent.
units.why: Assume Programming's transactions-isolation unit. This unit moves from database transaction interleavings to client-visible replica histories, where convergence and freshness are different contracts.

next.note: Turn the stated model into an independent history checker.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: consistency definitions and conflict intent
study.locator: Chapter 6, Problems with Replication Lag, pp. 209 to 214; Dealing with Conflicting Writes, pp. 222 to 227; Chapter 10, Linearizability and What Makes a System Linearizable?, pp. 402 to 408, including Linearizability Versus Serializability

study.title: Consistency Models: bounded definition review
study.locator: Sections 3.1 Linearizability, 3.3 Serializability and Strict Serializability, 4.1 Eventual Consistency, 4.2 Causal Consistency, and 5 Client-Centric Consistency Models
study.depth: Use after DDIA to label your histories. Skip the product-choice tables and quiz; do not treat the consistency spectrum as a total ordering of all guarantees.

focus: A linearization is a legal sequential object history that respects response-before-invocation order. Overlapping operations need not follow invocation order.

Serializability orders whole transactions but does not by itself require real-time order. Strict serializability adds it; per-object linearizability alone does not make a multi-object transaction atomic.
Eventual convergence needs propagation and a resolution policy. Read-your-writes and monotonic reads are session guarantees; causal consistency also preserves dependencies across clients.
LWW converges with a deterministic total timestamp order, but discards acknowledged updates. Sibling merge must preserve application meaning, especially deletion.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, check these register histories by hand, initially x=0 with no other writes. H1: P1 invokes write(x,1) at event 1 and receives OK at 2; P2 invokes read(x) at 3 and receives 0 at 4. It is not linearizable; if each operation is its own transaction, serializability alone permits the order read, write. H2: P1 invokes write(x,1) at 1 and receives OK at 4; P2 invokes read(x) at 2 and receives 0 at 3. It is linearizable in the order read, write. Separately, simulate two concurrent writes (timestamp=100,node=A,value=red) and (90,B,blue), comparing (timestamp,node): both arrival orders converge to red and discard blue. Merge cart siblings {book} and {dvd} by union after each device removed the other item from {book,dvd}; both deleted items reappear. Explain why convergence is not preservation of intent. Event numbers and timestamps are synthetic, not elapsed-time measurements.
traps: Using the phrase strong consistency without specifying the object, operations and real-time requirement.
Claiming eventual convergence bounds lag or guarantees durability.
Assuming set union correctly handles removals, or that LWW's greatest timestamp identifies the physically latest write.

selfTest.q: May a read overlapping a write return the old value?
selfTest.a: Yes, if a legal linearization places it before the write. Other completed observations can constrain that order.

selfTest.q: While write(1) is pending, read A returns 1; after A completes, read B returns 0. Is that linearizable if no other write exists?
selfTest.a: No. A forces the write before A, real time forces A before B, and then B must read 1.

selfTest.q: Does read-your-writes imply all users see the newest value?
selfTest.a: No. It constrains the writer's session, not arbitrary readers.

selfTest.q: P writes a post; Q reads it and writes a reply; R sees the reply but not the post. Which model rejects this?
selfTest.a: Causal consistency rejects visibility of the dependent reply without its causal predecessor. Eventual consistency alone does not reject a temporary lagging view.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: classify permitted and rejected histories, reproduce LWW data loss, and test an application conflict policy including removals.
units.stopWhen: You give legal orders for H2 and the merely serializable H1, reject H1 under linearizability, and explain a convergent merge that still violates application intent.

fit.note: DDIA defines the guarantees and conflict mechanisms; the pool's AlgoMaster review gives explicit causal and session vocabulary, with histories practised in the mini-project.
